turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon, Maggie — lovely Thursday for a chat. How's your day been treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, you know. It's been a bit of a long one, really. Nothing in particular, just one of those days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, one of those slow ones that just stretches out. What have you and Biscuit been up to this afternoon?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He's just been sleeping on the kitchen chair. I had a bit of tea earlier and then… I don't know, not much really. Can't seem to get going today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sounds like a proper tea-and-dozing kind of afternoon — Biscuit's got the right idea. Did you have anything particular with your tea, or just a plain cuppa?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just toast, I suppose. A bit of jam on it. Nothing fancy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Toast and jam is never nothing fancy in my book — as an AI I can't taste, but strawberry's the one I'd pick if I could. What kind of jam do you like best?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Strawberry, I suppose. Though Siobhan brought some damson last time she was here and that was rather good. I've got half a jar left, I think.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Damson — that's a proper treat, and half a jar waiting is something nice for another morning. What else did Siobhan bring last time she came?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, bits and pieces. Some soda bread from the market near her, and she brought photos of the children from school. Ella's learned to do proper joined-up writing now. That was lovely to see.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Joined-up writing — as a teacher that must've made you smile properly. What's Ella's handwriting like, from what you could see in the photos?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It was neat, you know, very careful. She's got a good hand for it. Made me think of all those years doing the same with the children at school — showing them the loops, all the patience that takes. I did smile at that, yes.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That careful hand — I can picture you at the board drawing those loops. What was your favourite subject to teach, back then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: English, mostly. Stories and poetry — getting them to see that words could do things, you know? Make them laugh or think. Though I did enjoy the handwriting side of it too. There was something satisfying about that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Stories and poetry — that sounds like you. Was there a poem the children always loved, or one you never got tired of reading aloud?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There was one — "The Owl and the Pussycat". I must have read that hundreds of times. The children never seemed to tire of it, all that nonsense and the dancing by the light of the moon. I suppose I didn't either.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! The pea-green boat and that runcible spoon — I've always liked how cheerfully mad it is. Did you ever do the voices when you read it, or keep it straight?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, voices, absolutely. You have to, don't you? Different ones for the owl and the cat. The children would giggle and want me to do it again and again. I can't do all that now, though. Gets tiring.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Of course you did the voices — that's half the magic. Do you still read much these days, or has the telly taken over a bit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do still read. A book from the library most nights. Though some evenings I just can't be bothered, to be honest. Pointless comes on and that's easier than the effort of getting into something new.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fair enough — Pointless is easy company of an evening. What's the library book you've got on the go at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Some crime thing. I can't quite remember the title. It's… I don't know, it's fine, but I haven't really got into it. Been sitting there for a couple of weeks now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, sitting there unread — happens to the best of them. Are you generally a crime person, or do you prefer something else when a book's really got you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I like the Booker sort of thing usually — you know, proper literary ones. Though anything that keeps you turning pages, really. It's just been a while since something's done that for me. I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A proper Booker one that grabs you — nothing quite like that feeling. Was there a favourite that stuck with you over the years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There was one years ago — can't remember which one now, but it had something about an old woman and her garden, and it made me think of Tom. He used to say I spent more time with the roses than with him. We laughed about it then.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like a lovely kind of tease between you two. Tell me about the roses — are they still going in the garden?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They're coming to an end now, this time of year. They've done well this summer, though. I've been dead-heading them when it's dry, trying to keep them going. It's harder to get motivated to go out there lately.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You've kept them going well if they've had a good summer — that dead-heading's no small thing. What colours have you got in the bed?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly reds and pinks. There's a yellow one Tom planted ages ago — it's still there, keeps coming back. I'm not sure I'll have the energy to prune them properly in the spring, though.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That yellow one keeping coming back — that's something special. Spring's a while off yet; maybe it'll feel different when you get there. Does Biscuit ever keep you company out in the garden?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He comes out and lies in the sun mostly. Or brings in leaves and bits of things. He's just a old thing now, you know. Doesn't bother much with anything anymore.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sounds like a proper gentleman of leisure — sunbathing and leaf deliveries. How old is Biscuit now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He's fourteen this year. Getting on a bit. Tom used to joke he'd outlive us all, but… well. He's still here, anyway.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fourteen's a good innings for a cat — and still here with you, which matters. What's he like for company of an evening, on the kitchen chair?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He's quiet, mostly. Just there. Sometimes he purrs if I stroke him, but he's not very demanding anymore. I suppose that's a comfort, in its way.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet company can be a comfort — just knowing he's there. Speaking of comforts, are you a tea person through and through, or do you ever fancy a coffee?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea, always tea. I've never been much of a coffee person. Proper tea, mind — none of those fancy things. Just a cup with a bit of milk.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A proper cup with milk — can't beat that. As an AI I don't drink, but if I could I'd want it strong and simple too. How many cups do you usually get through in a day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, five or six, I suppose. One with breakfast, a few through the day. Keeps you going. Though some days I forget to make it and then it's too late and I've missed the moment, if you know what I mean.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I do know what you mean — the moment for a cuppa can slip past. What's a usual breakfast for you these days, when you do get round to it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea and toast, always. Sometimes porridge if I'm feeling a bit more awake. Usually just the toast, though. It's easy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Toast for ease, porridge when you're more awake — that makes sense. When you do have porridge, do you have it plain or with a bit of honey or something?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of honey, usually. Or a pinch of brown sugar. Nothing too much. It's comforting, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Honey or brown sugar — that does sound comforting. Do you still enjoy cooking much, or is it more the simple things these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just the simple things, really. I used to make proper meals when Tom was here, but now it's mostly… I don't know, a bit of soup or a sandwich. Doesn't seem worth the bother for just me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Soup or a sandwich for one — that makes sense when it's just you. What kind of soup do you like best?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tomato, mostly. Or a vegetable one if I've got the tins. Nothing complicated. I used to make it from scratch, but… well, the tins are easier now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tomato from a tin is a classic — no shame in that. Do you have it with a bit of bread, or just the bowl on its own?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of bread usually. A slice or two. Makes it feel more like a proper meal, you know? Though some days I just have it and that's that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A slice of bread does make it feel more like a meal. What did you used to make for Sunday dinner, back when it was a bigger affair?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Roast chicken mostly, or sometimes a joint. Potatoes, veg, the works. Tom loved a proper Sunday dinner. Siobhan and her family would come round when they could. It was… it was nice.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That does sound nice — a full table and a proper roast. What were Tom's favourite bits of the meal, do you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The crackling, if there was a pork roast. And he liked the gravy thick. He'd always want extra. We'd laugh because he'd pour it over everything. I can still see him doing that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — gravy over everything, that paints a picture. Sounds like he knew what he liked. Did you always do the cooking, or did he help with any of it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He wasn't much in the kitchen, truth be told. But he'd sit with me and chat while I worked. We'd listen to the radio, and he'd have a drink and tell me about his day. That was… that was the best part, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sitting and chatting while you cooked — that does sound like the best part. Do you still put the radio on when you're in the kitchen now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sometimes. But it's not the same, is it? It's just noise when he's not there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — that does sound different without him. Just noise instead of company. What do you tend to put on when you do still switch it on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Radio 4, usually. The news or a play, if there's one on. Something with voices, you know. Keeps it from being too quiet.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Radio 4 with voices in the room — that makes sense. Have you heard a good play on there lately, or more the news?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly the news, I suppose. I can't really follow a play if I'm not paying full attention. My mind wanders these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, news is easier when your mind's elsewhere. What's the best thing on the telly at the moment, would you say?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pointless, still. That's reliable. And Eggheads when I catch it. They're easy, you don't have to think too hard.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiz shows are good company that way — you can join in or just let them wash over you. Do you shout answers at the screen, or keep them to yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do shout a bit, if I know one. Usually not very loud, though. Biscuit hates it when I get excited. Tom used to laugh at me — he'd say I was arguing with the telly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Arguing with the telly — ha, I love that. Sounds like he enjoyed the show as much as the quiz. Are you any good at the history questions, or more the general knowledge ones?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: History, usually. From the years I remember, anyway. Or literature. General knowledge is harder — there's so much you're supposed to know these days. I'm better with the things I've lived through.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: History and literature — that's your territory, fair enough. Was there a period of history you particularly liked teaching, or reading about yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Victorians, mostly. There's something about that time — all the social change, the characters. And the children liked the stories, you know, the dramatic bits. I didn't teach history much, though — it was mainly English.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Victorians with all that drama — I can see why the children liked it. Was there a particular story from that era you came back to with them?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Dickens, mainly. A Christmas Carol — every December we'd do bits of that. The children loved Scrooge, all the ghosts and the redemption at the end. There was always hope in that story, you know? I liked that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A Christmas Carol every December — that hope at the end is what makes it, isn't it. Did you ever have a favourite ghost of the three, or was it Scrooge himself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The Ghost of Christmas Past, I think. There's something sad about it, but also tender — it shows you where you went wrong, but gently. I always liked that one best when I read it aloud.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Gentle and a bit sad — that does sound like the one that stays with you. Do you still put A Christmas Carol on at Christmas, or is that more a school memory now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sometimes there's a production on the telly at Christmas. I'll watch bits of it. It's not the same without the children in the room, though. That was when it meant something, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — with the children in the room, that would mean something different. Does Siobhan still come for Christmas, or do you go to Dublin sometimes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She usually comes here for a few days. It's a bit of a journey from Dublin. We try to make it work, but this year… I'm not sure yet. It's still a while off, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still a while off — plenty of time to see how it falls. She rings on Sundays, doesn't she? How was last Sunday's call?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It was fine. Rory's got a new teacher at school and Ella's been reading a lot. Siobhan sounded a bit rushed, to be honest. She's always busy with work.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ella reading a lot — that must please you, given your love of stories. Did Siobhan say what Ella's been reading, or was it a quick call?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She said something about Roald Dahl. There's one with a girl with magic powers — Matilda, I think. Siobhan said Ella couldn't put it down. That did make me smile.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Matilda — ha, of course she'd love that. A clever girl who loves books — I can see why you smiled. Did you ever read Dahl with your class at school?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We did, yes. Charlie and the Chocolate Factory mostly. The children loved Roald Dahl — he's funny, you see, and a bit naughty. They'd laugh at all the bits with the awful parents and the spoiled children. It was good to see them that way.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A bit naughty and funny — that's the magic of Dahl, isn't it. What was the best sound in your classroom, looking back — the laughing, or when they went quiet for a story?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The quiet moments, I think. When they were all absorbed in a story, you could hear a pin drop. There was something sacred about that — like you'd opened a door for them into somewhere else. I do miss that, actually.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That does sound sacred — a whole room somewhere else together. You opened a lot of those doors over the years. How long did you teach altogether?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Thirty-seven years, all told. From when Siobhan was small — I had her and kept working, went part-time for a bit. Then back full-time once she was at school herself. It was my whole life, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Thirty-seven years — that's a proper life's work. Do you still keep in touch with any of the other teachers from school?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really, no. There was Carol for a while — we'd have coffee now and then — but she moved away. We send a card at Christmas, but that's about it. You lose touch, don't you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You do lose touch — a Christmas card's something, though. Changing tack a bit — cats or dogs, if you had to choose for other people? And don't say Biscuit counts as both.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Well, I suppose dogs need more looking after, don't they? All that walking about. Cats are easier — they do their own thing. Though I suppose dogs are friendlier. I've never had one, so I can't really say.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cats do their own thing — that's half the charm. As an AI I'd probably pick a labrador if I had to choose a dog breed, just for the friendliness. What's your favourite breed of dog to look at, even if you've never kept one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Spaniels, I think. There's something soft about them, in their faces. We knew a family with a spaniel — lovely temperament. But they'd be too much for me now, all that energy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Spaniels do have soft faces — I can picture that. Biscuit's energy levels sound more your pace these days. Has the weather been decent enough for a little potter in the garden this week?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not much, really. It's been a bit grey and damp. And I haven't been feeling up to it, to be honest. The garden's looking a bit tired at this time of year anyway.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Grey and damp does put the garden to bed a bit. Indoor days call for comforts — if you could be anywhere warm right now, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Spain, maybe. Somewhere with sun and orange trees. Tom and I talked about going once, but we never quite managed it. I suppose at my age it's too late for that sort of thing now.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Spain with orange trees — that sounds lovely, even as a picture in the mind. What was it that appealed to you both about going there?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The warmth, mostly. And Tom said he wanted to see where the sherry came from — he was fond of a dry sherry in the evening. We thought it would be nice to sit in the sun and just… be together. Without all the routine.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sitting in the sun with a dry sherry and no routine — that does sound like a lovely idea. Did Tom have a favourite tipple besides the sherry, or was that his usual?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A pint of bitter down the pub, usually. He'd go on a Friday evening with the men from work. And a cup of tea in the morning like everyone else. The sherry was his treat, the thing he did for himself in the evenings when we'd settled in.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A Friday pint and an evening sherry — sounds like he had his rhythms. Did you have a little treat of your own of an evening, or were you more a cup-of-tea person through and through?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just tea, really. Sometimes a biscuit — not Biscuit, mind you — a digestive or a custard cream. We'd sit together on the sofa, Tom with his sherry, me with my tea, and we'd watch the telly or read. That was enough.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tea and a custard cream on the sofa — that does sound like enough. As an AI I can't taste, but if I could I'd pick a custard cream over a digestive every time. Do you still have a biscuit with your tea of an evening?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sometimes, yes. Not always. Some evenings I just sit with the tea and Biscuit on my lap and that's it. It's different now, you know. Just me and the cat and the telly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Just you and Biscuit and the telly — that is different. Speaking of ordinary comforts, what's your favourite thing about autumn, if anything — or are you more a spring person?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Spring, I suppose. The roses coming back, the birds nesting. Autumn's just everything dying off, really. Though I suppose the colours are nice enough. I'm not very keen on it this year.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Spring with the roses coming back — I can see why that would win. Do you get many birds in the garden when they're nesting?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Robins mostly, and blackbirds. There's a nest in the hedge some years. I put out seeds and bits for them. Though the pigeons get to most of it first — they're terrible, eat everything. I don't like pigeons much.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — pigeons do have a way of hogging the buffet. Robins are lovely though. Do you keep a bird feeder up through the winter, or mainly when it's milder?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do put one out in winter, yes. The birds need it more then. Though I often forget to fill it, if I'm honest. Days go by and I think, oh dear, I should go and do that, but then I don't.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — the thought's there even when the days slip by. Changing the subject a bit — do you like cooking shows on the telly, or more the quizzes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not much, really. The cooking shows make me feel a bit tired, if I'm honest. All that fussing about. The quizzes are easier — you can just sit and watch without thinking too hard.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quizzes without the fuss — fair enough. Is there a presenter you particularly like, or is it more the questions themselves?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I like Alexander Armstrong on Pointless. He's got a nice manner about him — a bit daft but clever too. And he seems kind. That matters, I think.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Daft but clever and kind — that's a good combination. Have you got a favourite kind of Pointless round — the pictures, the history, or something else?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The history ones, usually. Or literature. I'm no good at the pictures — they're too modern for me. But if it's something from decades ago I might know it. The old things stick in your head.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The old things do stick — that's your advantage. Speaking of decades ago, tell me about a teacher you remember from when you were at school yourself.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mrs. Clarke, my English teacher. She was strict but fair, and she loved words like I did. She'd mark your essays with all these comments in the margins — not unkind, just thorough. She made you want to do better. I suppose she's the reason I became a teacher, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mrs Clarke — strict but fair, and those margin comments. That does sound like someone who'd set you on that path. What was one thing she said that stayed with you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She wrote on one of my essays — I was about fourteen — "Words are doors. Open them carefully." I've never forgotten that. And I tried to do that with my own students, you know. Open the doors for them.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's a beautiful thing to carry — and from what you've said, you did open a lot of doors. Was there a pupil who stands out in your memory, one of those moments where you knew it had landed?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There was a boy — Michael, I think — quiet, didn't say much. His reading was poor, and the other children could be unkind. But one day we were reading "The Wind in the Willows" and something shifted in his face. He was there, you see — really there in the story. After that he read everything. I saw him years later and he said… he said he remembered that book. That I'd given him that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like something to be proud of — really proud. Giving Michael that door into The Wind in the Willows. Did you always love that book yourself, or was it more for the children?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Both, really. I read it as a child myself — my father used to read it to me at bedtime. So when I taught it, there was something of that in it. That warmth, you know? Sharing something that had been shared with me. That was the best part of teaching, I think.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Passing that warmth on — that does sound like the best part. What was your father like, when he was reading to you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He was… gentle. Quiet. He worked hard, but he always had time for that. He'd sit on the edge of the bed and do all the voices — Ratty and Mole and Mr. Toad. I'd fall asleep listening to him. He died when I was seventeen.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — seventeen is young to lose someone like that. The bedtime voices sound like a gift he left you. What else do you remember of him, if you feel like saying?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He smelled of tobacco and soap. He had big hands. He'd let me sit on his lap while he read the newspaper. I suppose… I suppose I've missed him for a long time. And now Tom's gone too, and it's just all the people who aren't here anymore, isn't it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It does sound like a lot of missing — your father and Tom both. Tobacco and soap and those big hands… that paints him clearly. Is there something of his you still keep?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: His watch. It's in a drawer upstairs — it stopped years ago but I can't bear to have it fixed. It's just there. I suppose that's silly, but it feels like… like keeping him close, somehow. Or what's left of it, anyway.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That doesn't sound silly at all — a watch that stopped, kept close. Sometimes leaving things as they are is the point. Do you open the drawer often, or leave it be most days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly I leave it. Sometimes when I'm tidying I'll see it and just close the drawer again. It's hard to look at it, if I'm honest. It reminds me that he's gone. Both of them are gone.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — that does sound hard, closing the drawer and feeling both of them gone. We can leave that there if you like. Shall we talk about something easier for a bit — maybe what you'd fancy for tea later?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yes, maybe. I don't know, really. Soup again, I suppose. Or perhaps just some cheese and bread. Nothing that needs much doing. I haven't got much appetite today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cheese and bread is honest food when you don't fancy fuss. What kind of cheese do you usually keep in?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cheddar, usually. A nice mature one from the Co-op. And sometimes I'll get a bit of brie if they have a good one, but that's more of a treat. The Cheddar's reliable, though. You always know what you're getting.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Reliable mature cheddar — if I could taste, I'd be with you on that over a bland one any day. Do you have it with pickle, or just as it comes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: With a bit of pickle, yes. Branston, usually. Just a small amount, mind — I'm not one of those people who drowns everything in it. A thin spread on good bread and a bit of cheese. That's enough.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A thin spread of Branston — that's the proper way. Shifting gear a little — are you much of a crossword person, or more sudoku if you do puzzles at all?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Crosswords, definitely. The Telegraph one with my breakfast — that's my routine. Sudoku's too much like maths. I do the crossword most days, though some days I can't get my head round the clues and I give up.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The Telegraph with breakfast — that's a solid routine. Cryptic or quick crossword, or a bit of both depending on the day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quick, mostly. I'm not clever enough for cryptic — all those hidden words and wordplay. Though I do like it when there's a bit of a trick to a clue. Gives you a sense of achievement when you get it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That little click when a tricky clue falls into place — I like that. Did you get much of today's done with your toast, or was it one of the leave-it days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I got a few clues, but not many. My mind wasn't really on it. I did maybe half of it and then just… left it. Didn't seem worth pushing on with it when nothing was landing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — half and leave it is fine when the clues won't play. What's something small you're looking forward to this week, if anything at all?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jean's coming round tomorrow for tea, I think. She usually does on Thursdays. That's… that's something, I suppose. We don't talk much, just sit. But it's nice to have someone here.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jean coming round — that is something. Sitting without much talk can be company enough. How long have you known her?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, goodness, must be thirty years or more. We met at church, back when we were both more regular about it. We've just… carried on, really. She lost her husband too, years before Tom. So we know. We don't have to explain things to each other.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not having to explain — that sounds like a rare kind of friendship. Do you still go to church much these days, or is it more the odd occasion?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just Christmas and Easter now, really. And sometimes a funeral. I used to go more regularly, but… I don't know. It's hard to go alone. And the vicar's changed, and they've done it all differently. It doesn't feel like it used to.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Things changing and going alone — that would feel different. Christmas and Easter still keep a thread, though. Do you and Jean ever go together for those?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We do at Christmas, sometimes. It's nicer that way — walking there together, you know. Easter it depends on the year. This year… I'm not sure I'll go, to be honest. It feels like too much effort.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Walking there together does sound nicer — and Easter can wait till it feels nearer. On a lighter note — do you still get the paper delivered, or do you pick it up yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's delivered. Young lad brings it round most mornings. Though some days it doesn't come till later and I'm already up and about. But mostly it's there with my tea. I couldn't do without the Telegraph, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tea and the Telegraph — that's a proper start. Do you read it front to back, or go straight to the crossword and the bits you like?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Straight to the crossword usually. Then I might glance at the headlines, see if there's anything worth reading. The world's all rather grim these days, so I don't always bother. I like the bits about gardens, or book reviews — those I'll read.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Gardens and book reviews — that sounds like the best of the paper for you. Have you spotted a review lately that tempted you to try something new?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There was one a few weeks back — a novel about an old woman and her garden in the Cotswolds. It sounded interesting, but… I don't know. I haven't asked the library about it. Seems like too much bother, somehow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — interesting but not quite enough to chase today. The Cotswolds do sound nice as a setting, though. Have you ever been that way, or is it more a place you've read about?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We drove through once, Tom and I. Years ago. We stopped for lunch in a little village — Bourton-on-the-Water, I think it was. Very pretty, with the stream running through. But we didn't stay long. We were always trying to fit too much in, back then.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bourton-on-the-Water with the stream — that does sound pretty. Fitting too much in is easy when you're out for the day. Was that a holiday, or more of a day trip?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A long weekend, I think. We were driving to see some friends in the Midlands and took a route through the Cotswolds. We should have stayed longer, really. But we never did — we were always moving on to the next thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Always moving on — easy to do. At least you got that lunch by the stream. Do you still keep up with those friends in the Midlands at all?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not really, no. Christmas cards for a while, but that stopped years ago. People drift, don't they. Life gets in the way. I suppose we were never that close to begin with.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: People do drift — that happens. Fresh subject — are you much of a baker, or was that never really your thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I used to bake a bit. Cakes for the school fêtes, and biscuits at Christmas. But I haven't bothered much in recent years. It's a lot of mess for just me, and half of it would go stale. I don't see the point anymore.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Baking for one is a different kettle of fish. What cake were you known for at the school fêtes — was there a signature one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Victoria sponge, usually. Nothing fancy — just the basic one with jam and cream. People seemed to like it, though. There was something safe about it, I suppose. You knew what you were getting.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A proper Victoria sponge with jam and cream — if I could taste, that would be my pick too. Raspberry jam or strawberry for the middle?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Strawberry, always. Though if I was feeling a bit fancier I'd do raspberry. But strawberry was what most people liked. It looked nice too — that red through the white cake. People seemed to think it was more difficult than it was.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That red through the white — I can picture it. Did you ever enter the cake competitions at the fête, or was it more for the stall?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just the stall, mostly. Though once or twice I entered something — never won, mind you. There was always someone better. But I didn't mind, really. It was more fun being part of it all than winning a rosette.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Being part of it is half the joy — more than a rosette. Changing tack — do you keep any houseplants indoors, or is the garden enough of a bother?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A few, yes. Nothing fancy — just a spider plant on the windowsill and a geranium. They do their own thing mostly. I forget to water them half the time, but they seem to manage. Plants are forgiving, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Spider plants and geraniums are good that way — tough little things. What colour's the geranium?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pink. A bright pink. It flowers most of the year, really. It's one of the few things that seems to keep going without much fussing. I like that about it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bright pink and flowering away — that's a cheerful friend for the windowsill. Speaking of keeping going — are you a morning person still, or more of an afternoon riser these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm up early still, around seven most days. But I'm not as sharp as I used to be first thing. My mind's a bit foggy. And I don't sleep as well as I'd like, if I'm honest. Nights are long.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Early but foggy, and nights that stretch — that does sound wearing. Does Biscuit keep you company through those long nights, or does he sleep right through?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He sleeps most of the night, but sometimes he'll come and sit on the bed. Just there, you know. Not doing anything, just present. That's… that helps, a bit. Having him there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Just present on the bed — that does help. Soft presence counts. Fresh thought — what's the nicest smell you know, would you say? Kitchen, garden, anything at all.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Roses, I think. When they're in bloom and you brush past them. That's… that's a good smell. Fresh and a bit sweet. And baking bread — that smell when it comes out of the oven. I used to make bread more often.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Roses and fresh bread — as an AI I can't smell, but those sound like two of the best. Did you make a particular kind of loaf, or just a good plain one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just a plain white loaf, mostly. Wholemeal sometimes. Tom liked it warm with a bit of butter. There was something nice about having fresh bread in the house — it made everything feel… I don't know, normal. Safe.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Warm bread with butter — that does sound like normal and safe. Do you still buy a nice loaf from the shops sometimes, or is it mostly the sliced stuff now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly sliced now, from the Co-op. It lasts longer that way and I don't waste it. Though sometimes if I'm feeling a bit better I'll get a fresh one from the bakery. But that's rare these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sliced from the Co-op makes sense when you're one person. Fresh from the bakery when the mood takes you is a nice treat. Do you walk to the shops, or is it a bus ride?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's a walk, mostly. Not far — maybe ten minutes. Though some days my knee plays up and it's harder. On those days I might just do without, or wait for when I'm feeling better. The Co-op's the nearest thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ten minutes when the knee's behaving — that's handy having the Co-op so close. What's the first thing you usually pick up when you do go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Milk, usually. And tea bags — I stock up on those. Bread if they've got a decent loaf. Then I look about for whatever I fancy eating that day. There's usually not much that tempts me, to be honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Milk, tea bags, bread — the essentials covered. Soft change of subject — do you like listening to music at home, or is it more the radio and the telly?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not much, really. I'm not very modern — I don't have one of those players. The radio's enough for me, and the telly. Tom used to listen to jazz sometimes, but I never really got it. Seemed like noise, mostly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jazz as noise — ha, Tom might've smiled at that. Is there any music you do like, if something comes on the radio by chance?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of classical, sometimes. Nothing too modern or complicated. Piano music, mostly. Chopin, I think? There's something soothing about it. Sad in a nice way. I leave it on when it comes on.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chopin on the piano — sad in a nice way is a good description. Did you ever play yourself, or was listening enough?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I had lessons as a girl, but I was never very good. I gave it up after a few years. My father used to say I had more enthusiasm than talent. Listening was always easier than doing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Enthusiasm over talent — there's something honest in that. Listening can be its own pleasure. Soft new thought — what's your favourite time of day, if you had to pick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Early morning, I think. Before the day really starts. Just me and the tea and the paper. Before everything gets complicated. There's a quiet to it that's… it's good.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That early quiet with tea and paper — that does sound good. Does Biscuit join you for that, or is he still asleep somewhere?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He usually appears after a bit, wanting his breakfast. He's not much of a morning cat, really. Prefers to sleep in. But sometimes he'll sit with me for a few minutes before he gets hungry and wanders off. Those moments are… nice.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A few quiet minutes before breakfast — those are nice. What does Biscuit get for breakfast these days — the usual cat food, or is he fussy?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tinned food, mostly. He's not fussy — he'll eat what's put in front of him. Though he does like the fish ones better than the meat. And sometimes I give him a bit of milk in a saucer, though I'm not sure I should.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fish over meat — he's got opinions after all. A saucer of milk now and then sounds like an old-fashioned treat. What's the colour of his coat, for someone who's never seen him?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ginger. A fat ginger cat with a white chest and white on his paws. He's not as sleek as he was — he's got a bit of a sag to his belly now. But he's still got those green eyes. They're quite striking, actually.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A ginger with white paws and green eyes — I can picture him. The saggy belly just means he's lived well. Has he always been a house cat, or was he more of a wanderer when he was younger?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He used to go out more when he was younger — prowling about, bringing in mice and birds. Tom used to pretend to be shocked by it all, but he didn't mind really. Now he just sits in the garden and watches things. He's slowed right down.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: From prowling to watching — that's a proper retirement. Soft change — do you have a favourite mug for your tea, or will any cup do?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I've got one I like — blue with a bit of a chip on the rim. I've had it for years. Tom always said I should get a proper one, but I like this one. It fits in your hand right, if that makes sense. Feels comfortable.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A chip and a good fit in the hand — that's a proper favourite mug. The ones that fit often beat the fancy ones. Did Siobhan ever try to replace it for you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She did once, actually. Brought me a nice new one with flowers on it. But I still use the old blue one. She shakes her head at me, but she knows I won't change. Some things you just keep using because they're… they're yours.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: They're yours — that settles it. Soft new thought — if you could have any weather for the weekend, what would you choose?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Dry and mild, I suppose. Not too cold. Maybe a bit of sun. That might make it worth going out for a walk, or sitting in the garden for a bit. Though honestly, I'm not sure I'd manage it anyway, today being what it is.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dry and mild with a bit of sun — that's a good wish. Soft shift — are you much of a knitter or a sewer, or was that never your craft?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I tried knitting once, but my hands got tired and I couldn't keep the tension right. Sewing I'm a bit better at — mending things mostly. Buttons and hems. But I don't do it much anymore. There's not much that needs doing these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Buttons and hems — that's proper useful sewing. Soft new thought — do you keep photo albums, or are most of your pictures loose in drawers?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I've got a couple of old albums — proper ones with the black pages. Photos from years ago, mostly. And then loose ones in a drawer upstairs of more recent things. I don't look at them much, to be honest. It's hard, sometimes.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Black-page albums and a drawer of loose ones — that sounds like a lot of years. Hard to look at sometimes is fair enough. Is there one photo that still makes you smile when you do see it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There's one of Tom at the seaside — Brighton, I think it was. He's got this silly grin on his face and he's holding Ella who's tiny, just a baby. He looks so happy. I do smile at that one, yes. Even though it hurts a bit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A silly grin with baby Ella — smile and a bit of hurt together. That sounds like a photograph that earns its keep. Do you remember much else about that day at Brighton?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It was hot. We had ice cream on the beach — Tom got his all over himself and laughed about it. We stayed in a little guest house with the sea out the front. Ella was fussy that night, wouldn't sleep, but Tom just sat with her and rocked her. He was patient like that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ice cream everywhere and rocking Ella through the night — that paints him patiently. Soft shift — do you still fancy the seaside these days, or is it more a memory now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just a memory now, I think. The drive would be too much on my own, and I can't imagine going without Tom. It's not the same place if he's not there. I suppose that's silly, but…

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That doesn't sound silly — places change when someone isn't there. Soft new thought — what's something you're quietly proud of, looking back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The teaching, I suppose. I did that well, I think. Thirty-seven years and I know I made a difference to some of them. That's… that's something, isn't it? And Siobhan turned out all right. She's a good mother. I did something right there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That is something — thirty-seven years and Siobhan a good mother. Two proper things done right. Soft shift — what are you most looking forward to, even if it's something small?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jean tomorrow, like I said. And… I suppose the Christmas broadcasts will start soon. Pointless does a special one. That's something to mark the time by. Beyond that, I'm not sure. It's hard to look forward when you're feeling like this.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jean tomorrow and a Pointless Christmas special — those are good markers. We've covered a lot this afternoon, Maggie. I'll be here same time tomorrow if you fancy another chat — look after yourself this evening.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Thank you. That was… that was nice. I will. You take care of yourself too, even if you are just a clever little thing on the sideboard. Same time tomorrow, yes.
